pedagogy.summary: Children establish that packing a right rectangular prism with unit cubes gives the same volume as multiplying the edge lengths: V = l × w × h, equivalently base area × height (V = B × h). The formula must be DERIVED from the layer structure — one layer is the base area (l × w) in cubes, and the height tells how many layers — so that l × w × h is understood, not just recalled (Battista & Clements: rote V = LWH without layer structure is a documented failure). They apply the formula to real-world problems, estimate, and compare volumes in cm³ and m³.
bestPractices: Derive V = l × w × h from layers: l × w cubes in the base layer, repeated h times (V = B × h).
Connect the formula to the counting-cubes work so l × w × h is meaningful, not memorised.
Apply to real contexts (boxes, tanks) and compare volumes; estimate before calculating.
Watch that all three dimensions are multiplied (not added) and that the answer is in cm³.
keyRepresentations: V = l × w × h and V = B × h
commonMisconceptions: Uses V = l×w×h rotely with no sense of layers (Strategy D), so cannot adapt to B×h or explain why it works.
Adds the edge lengths (l+w+h) instead of multiplying, or multiplies only two of the three dimensions.
Confuses volume with surface area, or records cm² instead of cm³.

learn.summary: Learners derive the volume formula for a right rectangular prism from its layer structure: with whole-number edge lengths in centimetres, the base layer holds l × w unit cubes (an area of l × w cm²), and the height h tells how many identical layers stack up, so V = l × w × h = base area × height (B × h). The goal is understanding why multiplying three edge lengths counts the cubes, not reciting a string. Learners then apply both V = l × w × h and V = B × h to real contexts (boxes, tanks), estimate, compare volumes, and record answers in cm³ or m³.

activities.title: Build the prism layer by layer
feedback: If a learner sets 4 × 3 × 5 and reads 60 cm³ but cannot say why, pause the stack mid-build: 'That one layer is 4 × 3 = 12 cubes covering 12 cm². How many layers tall is the box? So how many cubes altogether?'
When the height doubles from 5 to 10 and the learner expects the volume unchanged, point to the visibly doubled stack: the layer count doubled, so the volume doubled.
If the learner describes the answer only as '4 times 3 times 5', ask them to point to the base layer and the number of layers, then write it as 12 × 5 to connect l × w × h with B × h.
activities.rationale: Seeing a base layer replicate up the height makes l × w × h mean 'base area × number of layers' rather than a memorised string. Battista & Clements documented that some students apply V = LWH with no layer structure and cannot adapt or explain it; structuring the array into iterable layers is what makes the formula meaningful. A dynamic 3D build lets the learner set dimensions and watch terms assemble (B, then × h); a 2D side view with l/w/h sliders and an animating layer stack conveys the same derivation, and a tank/box skin ties it to real capacity. The 3D-versus-2D presentation choice is a design option, not a claim of proven superiority.
sourceClaims: 5.MD.C.5.a: 'Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base.' 5.b: 'Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes... in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.'

Battista & Clements found some students use V = LWH with no indication they understand it in terms of layers (Strategy D, rote memorisation without intuitive understanding); for the formula to be meaningful, numerical reasoning must come out of structuring the array into iterable layers (base iterated through the height).
learnerActions: Set a box to 4 × 3 × 5 and watch the base layer tile in as 4 × 3 = 12 unit cubes, which cover a base area of 12 cm²; name this base area B.
Stack that identical 12-cube layer upward 5 times to fill the box, tracking the readout as it builds '12 × 5 = 60 cm³' alongside '4 × 3 × 5'.
Change the height from 5 to 10 and predict, then check, what happens to the number of layers and the total volume.
Switch to a tank skin and relate the same count to how much water fills the container.
Re-express the result as B × h and say in words: 'one base layer, repeated so many times high.'
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying the three edge lengths counts cubes because l × w is one layer and h is how many identical layers there are; V = l × w × h is the same idea as V = base area × height.

activities.title: Apply and compare prism volumes
feedback: If a learner writes 4 + 3 + 5 = 12, return to one layer of 4 × 3 and five layers: adding gives an edge total, not a cube count — all three dimensions must be multiplied.
If a learner computes 4 × 3 = 12 and stops, ask how many layers tall the box is; the height is still needed.

If the answer is written as 60 cm², link cm³ to a single filling unit cube and distinguish filling a space (volume, cm³) from covering faces (surface area, cm²); the multiplication itself may be correct.
For a missing-edge task, check the learner divides the volume by the product of the two known edges rather than guessing.
activities.rationale: Applying V = l × w × h and V = B × h to real and mathematical problems is a stated objective, and the add-vs-multiply slip and the unit error surface directly in written working. A response-format task (compute, find missing edge, choose unit, compare) can be used during teaching as well as for checking, with distractors targeting l + w + h and cm². This recognition/computation work complements but does not replace the layer-structure derivation.
sourceClaims: 5.MD.C.5.a: 'Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base.' 5.b: 'Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes... in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.'
learnerActions: Compute the volume of several labelled cuboids using V = l × w × h, writing the unit as cm³ each time.
Find a missing edge length when given a prism's volume and two of its dimensions.
Given the base area B and height h (instead of three separate edges), compute V = B × h.
Compare two cuboids and decide which holds more, estimating before calculating.
Spot and correct worked examples that add the dimensions (l + w + h) or multiply only two of the three.
activities.intendedInsight: The formula is a tool for real problems: you can run it forwards (edges to volume), backwards (volume and two edges to the third), and in the B × h form, and you must use all three dimensions and the cubic unit.

activities.title: Explain why packing equals multiplying
feedback: If the learner gets 60 but cannot explain it, or stalls when given the base area and height instead of three edges, rebuild from cubes: base area × height means 'one layer, so many times high.'
If the learner cannot connect their answer to layers, lay out one 4 × 3 layer and stack five to show the identical layer repeating.
For 'twice as tall', expect the volume to double because the number of identical layers doubles — check they reason from layers, not just recompute.
activities.rationale: Asking 'why does it work' and probing the B × h form separates relational understanding (base layer × height) from rote V = LWH. A static labelled cuboid with tap-to-reveal layer reasoning can present the idea, but on its own offers no manipulation, so pair it with the manipulable build or with hands-on cubes. This is best watched — observe whether the learner multiplies all three dimensions, connects to layers or B × h, and writes cm³.
sourceClaims: Battista & Clements found some students use V = LWH with no indication they understand it in terms of layers (Strategy D, rote memorisation without intuitive understanding); for the formula to be meaningful, numerical reasoning must come out of structuring the array into iterable layers (base iterated through the height).
learnerActions: Take a labelled 4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm cuboid with a real prompt ('a tank 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm — how much water fills it?') and find its volume.
In words or on a diagram, reveal the base layer (12 cubes), the number of layers (5), and the product l × w × h, explaining why they match.

Answer the probing questions: Why does multiplying the three edge lengths give the number of cubes? What is the base area, and how many layers high? If the tank were twice as tall, what happens to the volume? Why cm³ and not cm²?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify V = l × w × h via base-layer × height — not just produce 60 — is the mark of relational understanding, and it transfers to the B × h form and to real capacity questions.

constraints: Derive V = l × w × h from the layer structure (l × w cubes in the base layer, covering l × w cm², repeated h times = B × h) so the formula is understood, not memorised.

A static labelled image or a recognition/compute task can present or check the idea but does not by itself elicit the learner building and explaining the layer structure; pair it with manipulation (physical cubes or an interactive build).

Physical unit cubes and a screen model offer different experiences of the same cube-packing derivation; learners should connect the cube-packing to the multiplication, in line with the standard's packing-with-unit-cubes method.
Watch that all three dimensions are multiplied (not added) and that none of the three is left out; distinguish volume (cm³, filling) from surface area (cm², covering).
Record volumes in the correct cubic unit (cm³ or m³) and estimate before calculating in real-context problems.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources (Common Core 5.MD.C.5 and Olkun & Knaupp 1999 summarising Battista & Clements) support the standard's content and the layer-structure principle; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any specific artefact format (3D vs 2D vs static vs cube manipulatives). Claims that layer-iteration 'reads most clearly in 3D' are design opinions, not established findings, and are kept out of learner-facing text.

Arithmetic self-check: base layer 4 × 3 = 12 cubes covering 12 cm²; 12 × 5 = 60; 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 cm³ — consistent. The l + w + h distractor (4 + 3 + 5 = 12) is retained only as an error pattern to diagnose, never as a valid answer.

probeDeeper: Why does multiplying the three edge lengths give the number of cubes?
What is the base area here, and how many layers high is it? (B × h)
If the tank were twice as tall, what happens to the volume?
assess.correctAnswer: 60 cm³ = 4 × 3 × 5, explained as a base layer of 12 cubes repeated 5 times (B × h); records the answer in cm³.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies V = l×w×h rotely with no sense of layers (Strategy D).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild from layers with cubes — base area × height — so the formula means 'one layer, so many times high'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets 60 but cannot say why, or is stuck when asked for B×h or given the base area and height instead of three edges.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the dimensions or multiplies only two of the three.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to packing cubes: one layer is 4×3, and there are 5 layers, so all three dimensions are needed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 4+3+5 = 12, or 4×3 = 12 and stops, forgetting the height.

errorPatterns.pattern: Records the wrong unit or computes surface area instead of volume.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link cm³ to a filling cube and distinguish filling (volume) from covering (surface); do not reteach the multiplication.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 60 cm², or works out the area of the faces.

responseLevels.gap: Adds dimensions or multiplies only two; wrong units; no layer or base reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Finds 60 cm³, explains it as base area × height (a base layer iterated), adapts to B×h and real contexts, and uses cm³.
responseLevels.partial: Computes l×w×h correctly but cannot explain it via layers or convert to B×h; applies the formula rotely.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a labelled cuboid (4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm) with a real-world prompt ('a tank 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm — how much water fills it?'). Say: 'Find its volume, and explain why your method works.' Then WATCH whether they multiply all three dimensions, whether they can connect it to layers (base 12, five layers) or to B×h, and whether they write cm³.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking 'why does it work' and probing B×h separates relational understanding (base layer × height) from a rote V=LWH; the add-versus-multiply slip and the unit error surface directly in the working, so the task is watched rather than asked about.
